chunks: From him, from Habib ibn al-Hasan, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Hamid al-Attar, from Bashshar, from Zayd al-Shahham, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

A nabbash (grave digger/excavator) was captured in the time of Mu'awiya, so he said to his companions, 'What do you think?' They said, 'We will punish him and release him.' A man from the people said, 'Ali ibn Abi Talib did not do so.' He asked, 'What did he do?' He said, 'He would cut off the nabbash and said, 'He is a thief and one who uncovers the dead.'

key_terms.عَلِيُّ بْنُ أَبِي طَالِب: Ali ibn Abi Talib, the fourth Rashidun Caliph and first Imam
key_terms.مُعَاوِيَة: Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan, the Umayyad caliph
key_terms.نَبَّاش: A person who digs up graves to steal belongings
key_terms.يُقْطَع: He is cut off (referring to the punishment of amputation for theft)

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic legal ruling for a grave digger (nabbash) according to Imam Ali?
ai.summary: This hadith from *al-Istibsar* highlights the jurisprudential evolution of *hadd* punishment for grave robbers, contrasting the leniency of the Umayyad era under Mu'awiya with Imam Ali’s rigorous classification of the *nabbash* as a thief (*sariq*) due to the violation of the deceased's honor. By equating the grave with a repository of wealth, Ali’s ruling establishes the precedent for amputation, a view upheld in Shia fiqh as a deterrent against desecration. This ruling underscores the Shia emphasis on the continuity of rights (*huquq*) after death, linking physical theft to spiritual disrespect.
